items.title: Henry VIII had six wives — divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived
items.claim: What is the standard rhyme for Henry VIII's wives' fates?

options.text: 'Divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived' — Catherine of Aragon (annulled), Anne Boleyn (executed 1536), Jane Seymour (died after childbirth 1537), Anne of Cleves (annulled), Catherine Howard (executed 1542), Catherine Parr (survived him)

items.reveal_title: Six queens, three Catherines, two Annes
items.reveal:
Catherine of Aragon (m. 1509, annulled 1533, died 1536) was Henry's brother Arthur's widow. Anne Boleyn (m. 1533, executed 19 May 1536) bore Elizabeth I. Jane Seymour (m. 1536, died 24 October 1537) bore Edward VI.

Anne of Cleves (m. and annulled 1540) negotiated a comfortable settlement and lived until 1557. Catherine Howard (m. 1540, executed 13 February 1542) was perhaps 17 at marriage. Catherine Parr (m. 1543) outlived Henry (d. January 1547) and died in 1548.

The rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died' is a 19th-century mnemonic; Tudor contemporaries did not summarise the marriages this way.
items.why: Royal personal lives can carry constitutional weight. Henry's marital sequence drove the English Reformation, the succession crisis, and ultimately the Tudor dynasty's extinction with Elizabeth I in 1603.

items.title: Newton published the Principia in 1687

options.text: 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, deriving Kepler's planetary laws mathematically — uniting terrestrial and celestial physics
A defence of the Aristotelian universe
A treatise on biblical chronology only

items.reveal_title: Standing on the shoulders of giants
items.reveal:
The Principia was published in Latin in July 1687, funded by Edmond Halley after the Royal Society's stock of unsold fish books left it short of cash. Newton derived the inverse-square law of gravity, the three laws of motion, and applied them to planets, comets, the tides and the shape of the Earth.

Newton had developed calculus (his 'fluxions') in 1665-66 during the plague closure of Cambridge. He published Opticks in 1704 in English.

Newton became Master of the Mint in 1699, prosecuting counterfeiters. He served as President of the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727. His tomb is in Westminster Abbey.
items.why: Modern physics begins with one book. The unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics in 1687 is the high-water mark of the Scientific Revolution — and remained the framework of physics until Einstein.
